notes: West leads the ♥J against 6♠. After the defense takes the ♥A and continues the suit, South's only problem is how to play the trump suit for no losers. The correct play is to finesse East for the ♠K. That play is superior to cashing the ♠A on the first round (see hand A-3 on skill level 2).

South must be careful how he manages the spade finesse. After crossing to the dummy in diamonds, it would be wrong to lead a low spade from dummy and finesse with the ♠J. After that start, it would be impossible to pick up the suit if East started with all 3 spades.

South should instead begin by leading the ♠Q from the dummy intending to pass it. When East covers with the ♠K, South wins the ♠A. South crosses back to the dummy in diamonds. A finessing position now exists over East's ♠10.
South has nothing to lose by playing spades in this way. Picking up all 3 spades in East's hand is what can be gained.

South must decide at once which suit is the most likely source for his thirteenth trick. West's diamond opening has put the lead in the dummy for the first and last time. South must cash dummy's other diamond winner and discard appropriately from the closed hand.
The correct decision should be made based on probabilities. The odds of a suit breaking 3-3 are about 36%. The odds of a finesse working are 50%.
South should, therefore, plan to take the heart finesse. He should discard the ♠2 on dummy's second diamond honour and play a heart to the ♥Q. When East has the ♥K, South has all 13 tricks.

notes: West's lead of the ♠6 must be from a 4 card suit. Players conventionally lead their fourth best card from a broken holding. As the ♠6 is the lowest outstanding spot card in spades, West must have only 4 spades.

South still has nothing to lose by holding up the ♠A until the second round. South has 8 top tricks (the ♠A, the ♥A, 2 diamond tricks, and 4 club tricks). South must decide whether to try for his ninth trick in hearts or in diamonds.

South cannot afford to combine his chances in hearts and diamonds. If South cashes the ♦K and ♦A and finds diamonds breaking 4-1, it will be too late to play on hearts. The defense will be able to cash 2 spade tricks and 2 diamond tricks in addition to a heart trick.

Some bridge problems can be solved only by using probabilities. 3 diamond tricks can be taken if that suit divides 3-2. A 3-2 break will occur about 68% of the time. An extra trick in hearts can be taken if West has either the ♥K or the ♥Q or both honours. West will have 1 or more heart honours about 76% of the time. It is, therefore, superior to play on hearts.
South leads a low heart and when West follows low, so does dummy. East can win the trick and the defense will cash their spades.
After regaining the lead, South leads another low heart. If West follows low, another finesse is taken. When East can only produce a low card, South has his ninth trick.

Bridge players should have a good working knowledge of probabilities of suit breaks and honour distributions. Many bridge books contain tables of important bridge odds. Memorizing a handful of numbers can help solve most problems like this one.

notes: West leads the ♦J against 6♠. South has 1 loser in both hearts, and diamonds. South must plan to ruff his heart loser in the dummy after discarding North's ♥4 on South's third club winner. East's ♦J lead might be a singleton. South should time his plays so that East will not be able to lead diamonds through South's trump holding, promoting a trump trick for the defense.

After winning the opening diamond lead, South should draw just 1 round of trump. Next should come the ♥A, followed by 3 rounds of clubs for a heart discard. South can now ruff his heart loser in the dummy.
North still has a trump remaining so that South can easily draw the outstanding trump.

Notice that if South had drawn another round of trump earlier, he would be forced to lead a diamond from the dummy. East could win the diamond trick and promote West's ♠J into the setting trick by playing another diamond.

notes: West leads the ♦Q against 4♠. South must lose a trick to the ♠A. A heart loser is also certain. There are also losers in both diamonds and clubs.

In order to hold his losers to 3, South must try to develop a heart trick in North's hand. South must be quick to establish North's heart suit. If South tries to play trumps first, the defense will win the ♠A and continue diamonds or clubs to knock out an entry to the North hand. South will no longer be able to do anything with North's heart suit.

South should win the ♦A and lead the ♥2, conceding a heart trick. The defense will win this trick and return either clubs or diamonds. Declarer wins the ♣A or ♦K in dummy and leads a heart from North.

If East plays the other high heart honour, South can ruff. He can later get rid of at least one of his losers on dummy's good hearts. If East plays low on North's heart lead, South discards from the minor in which the defense has set up a trick. South may lose a second heart trick, but dummy's hearts are now good and will provide a discard for South's other minor suit loser.

notes: South wins the opening spade lead and must play on clubs to come to 9 tricks. As South has only 1 more spade stopper, he cannot afford to lose the lead more than once in clubs.

South should play a club towards dummy at trick 2. When West follows low, South must decide which club to play from North. The ♣A should not be considered. The choice is between the ♣Q and the ♣10 (or any other low card in clubs).

If clubs are 3-3, the ♣Q will work when West has only the ♣K. The ♣10 will work when West has only the ♣J. These 2 chances are the same. If both club honours are together South's choice is irrelevant.

If East has 4 clubs, again it doesn't matter what South does. If West has 4 clubs to the ♣J, South cannot succeed. If West has 4 clubs to the ♣K, the ♣Q must be played from dummy. The ♣Q is also a winner if East has a singleton ♣J.
Since playing the ♣Q picks up more holdings, South should, therefore, play the ♣Q at trick 2.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 4♠. South has 5 possible losers (2 in hearts, the ♦A, and 2 in clubs). It would be a mistake to allow West to win the opening club lead as a heart shift would not be welcome.

North's diamond suit should provide ample discards for South's losers once the ♦A is dislodged. It would be a mistake for South to draw trump at once. West would then be in a position to duck the ♦K lead, leaving South with 4 certain losers.

The ♠J is needed as a dummy entry. Thus, after winning the ♣A, South should play his ♦K at once. Now it does West no good to duck. South crosses to the ♠J and concedes a diamond trick to West, discarding a loser. The ♥A is still a dummy entry to dispose of another loser from South's hand on the established diamonds in North's hand.

The correct play is to lead any spade (including the ♠Q) out of the closed hand and, if West follows small, play low from dummy. On the given lie of the cards, South is immediately successful.

If East is able to win the trick cheaply, South wins the return and takes a second spade finesse. If East discards, South can take a third spade finesse. The last trump is drawn and South easily takes the balance.
Remember, when playing a 4-4 fit missing just the King and Jack for 1 loser, the best play is to double finesse.

There is one danger. If South plays the ♠3 at trick 1 from the dummy, East may have the ♠Q which will force South's ♠A.
The defense will hold up the ♣A until the second round, leaving South without an entry to cash out that suit.
South can ensure his contract by playing North's ♠K at trick 1. South knocks out the ♣A and still has the ♠A to reach his remaining club winners.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 3NT. After the defenders set up their spades, South must hope to play clubs for 5 tricks. The ♠A, ♥A, ♥K, and ♦A will make up the rest of South's 9 tricks.

If clubs are 3-2, the contract will make easily. If East has 4 or more clubs, the contract has no hope. If West has four clubs to the ♣J and ♣10, South cannot take 5 club tricks without jeopardizing the contract on more normal 3-2 club breaks.

South can make the contract with careful play if West has 4 clubs with only 1 of the ♣J and ♣10. South must play the ♣9 on the first or second round of the suit. If South saves the ♣9 until the third round, he will have a finessing position over West's club honour, but the club suit will be blocked. West will not cover when South leads the ♣9 and dummy's clubs will be stranded.
If South unblocks the ♣9 on the first or second round, he will be able to finesse against West's honour and enjoy dummy's long clubs.

notes: West leads the ♠K which South wins in dummy. West's spade lead creates a third possible loser for South. The ♥A must be lost and a diamond loser looks certain.
Since West has shown the ♠Q with his lead of the ♠K, South has a line of play available that is certain to succeed. South should play 2 rounds of clubs, discarding dummy's ♠2 on the second round.

South now has a ruffing finesse position available in spades. South leads a spade out of his hand, discarding a diamond from dummy if West follows low. South continues spades, ruffing in dummy whenever West plays the ♠Q.
South will have enough spade winners left to take care of the rest of dummy's diamond losers. The ♥A will be the only trick for the defense.

South needs 4 tricks in diamonds. The ♦K must be with West, but South must take care in playing the suit. If South leads the ♦Q out of his hand, West will cover with the ♦K. If diamonds are not 3-3, the defense will have a diamond stopper.
By proper play, South can also succeed when West has the ♦K and less than 3 diamonds. South begins by playing a low diamond towards dummy, finessing when West follows low.
South crosses back to his hand in clubs and plays his other low diamond towards the dummy. If West started with doubleton King of diamonds, he will play the ♦K and South will have his 9 tricks.
If West follows low, South finesses again and will need diamonds to be 3-3. South cannot succeed if West has 4 or more diamonds to the ♦K.

East will win the ♠A and play spades, allowing West to ruff out the ♠J. South has lost 2 tricks and still has a spade loser. The contract will depend on the diamond finesse. That finesse will probably lose as East rates to have the ♦K for his overcall.

If South plays low from dummy at trick 1, the defense has no recourse. If East ducks, West may switch to diamonds, but South is in control. South takes the ♦A and draws trump, eventually surrendering tricks to the ♠A and ♦K. Dummy will have a diamond winner to take care of South's club loser.
If East had taken his ♠A at trick 1 and given West a ruff, South would have 2 spade tricks and 10 top tricks. South should win the diamond shift, draw trump, and cash his 10 tricks.

notes: West leads the ♦5 against 6♥. With an almost certain trump loser, the diamond finesse represents the best chance of making the contract. Accordingly, South should finesse North's ♦Q at trick 1.

When East wins the ♦K and returns a diamond, South must play the heart suit for no losers. There is only one hope. One of the defenders must hold doubleton Queen and Jack of hearts. The ♥A and ♥K will drop the ♥Q and ♥J. The ♥10 will then be high and it can be used to draw the last trump.

When South leads a small heart off the dummy and East follows with the ♥Q or ♥J, South should not be tempted to finesse the ♥9 on the second round. If East was dealt a singleton honour in hearts, West will always have a heart trick. If East was dealt honour doubleton in hearts, he could have guaranteed a defensive heart trick by playing low.

notes: The defense starts with 3 rounds of hearts. South is forced to ruff as the ♦A must be lost. If South tries to draw trump immediately, he may go down when trumps break 4-2.
South cannot draw 4 rounds of trump because that would also exhaust his own trump supply. The defense might be able to cash hearts when they win the ♦A.

Drawing 2 or 3 rounds of trump before playing on diamonds could be equally fatal. Not only does a defensive diamond ruff become possible, but West may be able to win the ♦A and make South ruff another heart. East will have more trumps than South and the contract will fail.

South should not draw trump at all before attacking diamonds. If the defense persists in hearts, North's trumps can take care of the ruff. South can draw all the outstanding trumps and take the balance.

If West has the ♦A and East the ♦Q, it is necessary to play the ♦K from dummy. This play will lose if West has the ♦Q and East has the ♦A.

The above layout is impossible. West opened the bidding with 1NT showing 15-17 high card points. As the defense has only 18 high card points in total, West can have a maximum of 14 points without the ♦A.
West must have the ♦A. Therefore, the ♦K from dummy is the correct play.

notes: The defense takes the first 2 spade tricks and switches to diamonds. South has at least 1 certain loser in clubs and, therefore, cannot afford to misguess diamonds.
It is necessary to assume that West has the ♣A. If East holds that card, there will be 2 club losers and the contract will have no chance.

Once the assumption about the ♣A is made, the position of the diamond honours can be inferred. If West had the ♦A in addition to the ♠A and ♠K already shown, and the ♣A we are assuming he has, he would have 15 points, enough to open 1NT. If West's hand was unbalanced, preventing him from opening 1NT, he surely would have competed more vigorously in the bidding.
If we assume that West has the ♣A, it is almost a sure thing that East has the ♦A. South should, therefore, play the ♦J from dummy.
When South regains the lead, he can draw trump and lead clubs twice towards the dummy.

notes: The defense starts by cashing 3 rounds of hearts. West leads a fourth round of hearts and East ruffs, killing North's heart winner.

South should overruff with a trump other than the ♠4. If South overruffs with the ♠4, he will never be able to reach dummy in spades. After ruffing high and drawing trump, South must decide how to get rid of his diamond losers.

If West has the ♦K, he can be finessed for that card. South can later trump his third diamond in the dummy. It is very unlikely that West has the ♦K. West passed originally but has already shown up with 9 points in hearts and a singleton in spades. If West also had the ♦K, he almost certainly would have opened the bidding.

By similar thinking, the inference is even stronger that East has the ♣A. Declarer should plan on taking a ruffing finesse against that card. South should play the carefully preserved ♠4 to the dummy and lead clubs through East.

If East plays low, South can discard a diamond and repeat the play in clubs. Whenever East plays the ♣A, South ruffs and crosses to the ♦A. Dummy's now good clubs can be used to discard whatever diamond losers South has left.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. South might as well hold up the ♥A for 3 rounds. Even after this hold up, it is too dangerous to play on diamonds. It is very likely that the defense will be able to win the ♦A and run the heart suit.

South should play on clubs, finessing West for the ♣K. It looks very natural to start that suit with the ♣Q. South will be sorry, however, if West was dealt a singleton ♣K. East's club holding will be promoted into a stopper.
South should instead play the ♣2. If West has the singleton ♣K, the ♣Q, ♣J, and ♣10 will take care of the rest of East's clubs.

If West plays low on the ♣2, South plays the ♣10 or ♣J from dummy. South can cross to his hand in spades and play the ♣Q through West. As long as West has no more than 3 clubs to the ♣K, South cannot be prevented from running that suit. If West refuses to cover the ♣Q, the ♠A will be an entry to dummy's clubs.

The other 4-1 trump breaks are the relevant cases. It seems natural for South to play a high spade at trick 2. South can later cross to the dummy and lead a spade towards the closed hand. This line of play will fail when East started with a singleton spade honour. There are 3 possible singleton spade honours (the ♠A, ♠K, and ♠Q) that East could have.

South improves his chances slightly by leading a low spade out of the closed hand. This play will lose when West has a singleton small spade. Since there are only 2 singleton small spades (the ♠8 and ♠7) that West could have, this is a superior line of play.

notes: West leads the ♣5 against 3NT. South has 7 top tricks (3 spades, 2 hearts, the ♦A, and the ♣A). South can establish 2 more tricks in diamonds even if West has the ♦K and the finesse loses.

The only possible problem is that the defense might be in a position to cash 4 club tricks when West wins the ♦K. If South ducks the opening club lead, East may win the trick with a doubleton honour. East will return the suit and West will cash 3 more club tricks when he wins the ♦K.

South can virtually guarantee his contract by playing the ♣A at trick 1. If East has a doubleton honour, he can either play low, blocking the defensive clubs, or play high giving South a second stopper.
If the clubs were 4-3, the contract was never in danger. If West was dealt 5 clubs to the ♣K, ♣Q, and ♣J, he would have led the ♣K.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 4♠. South appears to have only 3 losers, the ♠A and 1 trick each in diamonds and clubs. West's heart preempt, showing great length in the suit, should alert South to a possible danger. East may be able to ruff the ♥A.
South has a simple remedy to this problem. South should duck the opening lead in the dummy. The ♥A can be used later to pitch a loser from the South hand.

West may switch to a diamond. South should win the ♦A and play on trumps. East wins the ♠A, cashes a diamond trick, and switches to clubs. South must take care to win this trick in the closed hand. South can draw the remaining trumps and use the ♣K as an entry to dummy. South's club loser can be discarded on the ♥A.
